body:
The French East India Company

The French East India Company was established in 1664 under the patronage of the French monarchy. Jean-Baptiste Colbert, a minister of Louis XIV, played an important role in its formation.

The French established commercial interests at Surat and Masulipatnam before developing important settlements at Pondicherry and Chandernagore.

Francois Martin is associated with the establishment and early development of Pondicherry, now Puducherry, from 1674. Pondicherry became the principal French administrative and political centre in India.

Chandernagore, in Bengal, developed into an important French commercial establishment around 1690. Other French settlements included Mahe, Yanam and Karaikal.

Why the English and French became military rivals

During the 18th century, English and French trading interests increasingly overlapped in southern India. Both companies sought commercial privileges, protected settlements and influence over Indian rulers.

The declining authority of the Mughal Empire allowed regional rulers to exercise greater independence. Disputes over succession in Hyderabad and the Carnatic created opportunities for European companies to support rival claimants.

European forces could provide military assistance to a claimant and, in return, seek money, territory or commercial privileges. The companies therefore became participants in Indian political disputes.

The 3 Carnatic Wars

First Carnatic War, 1746–1748

The First Carnatic War was connected with the War of the Austrian Succession in Europe. The French captured Madras in 1746.

The conflict ended through the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748. Madras was restored to the English.

This war demonstrated that European military conflict could directly affect trading settlements in India. It also exposed the growing political importance of European armed forces in southern India.

Second Carnatic War, 1749–1754

The Second Carnatic War developed principally from succession disputes in Hyderabad and the Carnatic.

Joseph Francois Dupleix, the French governor at Pondicherry, supported claimants who could strengthen French influence. The English supported rival political interests.

Robert Clive's capture and defence of Arcot in 1751 became an important English military success. Dupleix was recalled to France in 1754.

The central distinction is that the Second Carnatic War was strongly connected with Indian succession politics, whereas the First and Third Carnatic Wars were closely linked with major European wars.

Third Carnatic War, 1756–1763

The Third Carnatic War formed part of the wider Seven Years' War between European powers.

The decisive battle was the Battle of Wandiwash in 1760, in which English forces under Sir Eyre Coote defeated the French forces commanded by Count de Lally.

The English subsequently captured Pondicherry in 1761.

The Treaty of Paris in 1763 ended the wider conflict. French settlements were restored for commercial purposes under restrictions that prevented France from rebuilding a comparable independent political and military position in India.

Why the English became the dominant European power

The English benefited from stronger maritime support and greater capacity to obtain reinforcements. Their commercial resources and growing political position, especially in Bengal after 1757, also supported military operations.

The French depended on support from France and faced difficulties maintaining sufficient naval and financial resources in India. These disadvantages became particularly important during the Third Carnatic War.

French defeat did not mean the disappearance of French settlements

The English victory at Wandiwash and the Treaty of Paris ended France's serious challenge to English territorial supremacy in India. They did not mean that every French settlement permanently disappeared. French commercial establishments continued to exist.

Prelims focus

  • 1664: French East India Company established.
  • 1674: Francois Martin associated with the establishment of Pondicherry.
  • 1748: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle ended the First Carnatic War.
  • 1751: Robert Clive's success at Arcot during the Second Carnatic War.
  • 1760: Eyre Coote defeated Lally at Wandiwash.
  • Trap: Wandiwash was fought in 1760; the Treaty of Paris was concluded in 1763.

[Sources: IGNOU, Rise of Regional Powers, Unit 1, Section 1.5.2, Anglo-French Struggle in South India, consulted 20 November 2026; IGNOU, Eighteenth Century Politics: II, Unit 19, discussion of the 3 Carnatic Wars, consulted 20 November 2026; IGNOU, Colonial Expansion and Indian Resistance–I, Unit 3, Sections 3.3–3.7, consulted 20 November 2026; Bibliotheque nationale de France, France–South Asia Shared Heritage, Bengal, history of French establishments in Bengal, consulted 20 November 2026.]

body:
The political position of Bengal in the 18th century

The Mughal Empire weakened after the death of Aurangzeb in 1707. Provincial governors and powerful regional groups increasingly controlled political and financial affairs within their territories.

Bengal emerged as an important regional state under rulers such as Murshid Quli Khan, Alivardi Khan and Siraj-ud-Daulah.

Bengal possessed a prosperous agricultural economy, important textile production centres and valuable commercial routes. Its resources attracted European trading companies, including the English East India Company.

Why the Company came into conflict with Bengal's nawabs

The Company wanted greater freedom to conduct trade, enlarge its settlements and protect commercial establishments through fortification. The Bengal nawabs sought to maintain their authority over customs duties, fortifications and political affairs.

The main causes of disagreement were:

  • Customs duties: The Company claimed commercial exemptions. Company employees engaged in private trade sometimes attempted to use these privileges without paying the duties otherwise applicable to their transactions.
  • Fortifications: The Company strengthened its settlements without always obtaining the required permission from the Nawab.
  • Political interference: Company officials attempted to influence court politics and favoured rulers who would grant additional commercial privileges.
  • Territorial authority: The Nawab objected to Company conduct that reduced his control over trade and administration.

These disputes were not simply disagreements over the prices of goods. They concerned the authority to make and enforce decisions within Bengal.

Siraj-ud-Daulah and the crisis of 1756

Siraj-ud-Daulah became Nawab of Bengal in 1756 after the death of Alivardi Khan.

He demanded that the English Company stop unauthorised fortification, cease interfering in political affairs and respect revenue obligations.

When these disagreements remained unresolved, Siraj-ud-Daulah attacked Company establishments. His forces captured the English factory at Kasimbazar and then Calcutta in 1756.

The Company responded by sending military forces from Madras under Robert Clive, supported by naval forces.

The Battle of Plassey, 23 June 1757

The Battle of Plassey was fought at Palashi in Bengal between the English East India Company under Robert Clive and the forces of Siraj-ud-Daulah.

A decisive factor was the Company's agreement with Mir Jafar, one of the Nawab's senior military commanders. Mir Jafar expected to become Nawab if Siraj-ud-Daulah was defeated.

During the battle, Mir Jafar and important sections of the Nawab's army did not actively support Siraj-ud-Daulah. The Company achieved victory.

Siraj-ud-Daulah was subsequently captured and killed. Mir Jafar became Nawab of Bengal with Company support.

Why Plassey was decisive

Plassey gave the East India Company decisive influence over the selection and conduct of Bengal's Nawab. The Company did not immediately replace the entire Nawabi administration with direct territorial rule. Instead, it exercised increasing control through a ruler who depended heavily on its support.

From Mir Jafar to Mir Qasim

Mir Jafar became Nawab in 1757 but faced increasing Company demands for money and commercial concessions. Relations deteriorated when he could not satisfy these demands.

The Company replaced Mir Jafar with Mir Qasim in 1760. Mir Qasim attempted to restore the Nawab's independent authority and reduce the Company's interference.

The conflict with Mir Qasim eventually led to a larger military confrontation at Buxar in 1764.

Why Plassey mattered beyond Bengal

Before Plassey, the English Company relied mainly on trade and political permission for its commercial activities. After Plassey, it gained considerable influence over a wealthy regional state.

That influence helped the Company obtain additional resources and military advantages. Bengal subsequently became an important base for further British territorial expansion.

Prelims focus

  • 1707: Death of Aurangzeb, followed by growing autonomy of regional powers.
  • 1756: Siraj-ud-Daulah became Nawab of Bengal.
  • 23 June 1757: Battle of Plassey.
  • Robert Clive commanded Company forces; Siraj-ud-Daulah was the opposing Nawab.
  • Mir Jafar became Nawab after the Company's victory.
  • Trap: Mir Jafar is associated with Plassey; Mir Qasim is associated with the later conflict culminating in Buxar.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 11–14, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, pp. 138–146, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, Rise of Regional Powers, Unit 1, Section 1.5.3, Conquest of Bengal: Plassey to Buxar, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: The Conquest of Bengal: Conflict with the Nawabs and the Battle of Plassey

body:
Why conflict continued after Plassey

Although the Company had gained major political influence after Plassey, it continued to rely on the Nawab's administration and demanded additional financial and commercial privileges.

Mir Jafar could not satisfy all these demands and was replaced by Mir Qasim in 1760.

Mir Qasim attempted to strengthen Bengal's administration and armed forces. He also opposed the Company's misuse of commercial privileges.

The dispute over duty-free trade

Company employees used commercial permits, often called dastaks, to claim exemptions from customs duties. Their private trade frequently benefited from privileges that Indian merchants did not enjoy on the same terms.

Mir Qasim attempted to reduce this inequality and protect the Nawab's revenue authority. In 1763, he abolished internal customs duties in Bengal to place merchants on a more equal footing.

The Company's leaders resisted arrangements that weakened their privileged commercial position. The disagreement escalated into armed conflict, and Mir Qasim was displaced.

The alliance against the Company

Mir Qasim sought support from other Indian rulers. A coalition emerged involving:

  • Mir Qasim: The displaced Nawab of Bengal.
  • Shuja-ud-Daulah: The Nawab of Awadh.
  • Shah Alam II: The Mughal emperor.

The combined forces confronted the English East India Company at Buxar, in present-day Bihar, on 22 October 1764.

The Company forces were commanded by Hector Munro. The Company won a decisive military victory.

Plassey and Buxar compared

FeaturePlasseyBuxar
Year17571764
Company commanderRobert CliveHector Munro
Principal opponentsSiraj-ud-DaulahMir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II
Immediate significanceCompany gained decisive influence over Bengal's Nawab.Company defeated a coalition including the Mughal emperor and Awadh.

Both battles strengthened the Company, but they did so in different ways. Plassey established political influence in Bengal, while Buxar demonstrated wider military superiority over important regional and imperial forces.

The Treaty of Allahabad, 1765

Following the Battle of Buxar, settlements were concluded at Allahabad in 1765.

The Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the East India Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, now commonly spelt Odisha.

Diwani

Diwani meant authority over the revenue and financial administration of a province. The grant allowed the Company to collect and use revenues from Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

The Diwani grant was not another battlefield victory. It was a formal imperial grant that followed the Company's military success at Buxar.

The Nawab retained nominal responsibility for other aspects of government, while the Company's control of revenue made it the dominant power. This arrangement is commonly associated with the system of dual government in Bengal after 1765.

Why revenue rights strengthened the Company

Before gaining control over Bengal's revenues, the Company needed substantial supplies of bullion, especially silver, to purchase Indian goods.

After obtaining the Diwani, it could use revenue collected in India to purchase goods, pay soldiers and support its expanding administration and military campaigns.

Thus, commercial privileges, political influence, military victory and revenue collection became connected. This strengthened the Company's ability to conduct further campaigns against Indian states.

Keep the 3 stages separate

  • 1757: Plassey increased Company influence over the Nawab of Bengal.
  • 1764: Buxar established military superiority over a wider Indian coalition.
  • 1765: The Diwani grant provided authority over the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

Prelims focus

  • 22 October 1764: Battle of Buxar.
  • Hector Munro commanded the victorious Company forces.
  • Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II formed the opposing coalition.
  • 1765: Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
  • Diwani concerned financial and revenue administration.
  • Trap: The Mughal emperor fought on the opposing side at Buxar, not at Plassey.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 13–14, and Chapter 3, Ruling the Countryside, p. 26, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, Rise of Regional Powers, Unit 2, Section 2.4.2, Buxar and After, consulted 20 November 2026; Directorate of Census Operations, Bihar, District Census Handbook: Buxar, Census of India 2011, introductory historical section on the Battle of Buxar, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Before 1765, imported bullion bought Indian goods; after Diwani, Indian revenue funded textiles, Company troops and administration.
pictures.caption: How the Diwani changed the financial basis of Company power.

title: The Battle of Buxar and the Diwani of 1765: From Political Influence to Revenue Power

body:
Mysore emerges as a powerful regional state

Mysore became an important military and commercial power in southern India during the 18th century.

Haidar Ali established effective control over Mysore in 1761 and ruled until 1782. His son, Tipu Sultan, ruled from 1782 until 1799.

Mysore's military strength and its control over commercially important territories brought it into conflict with the English East India Company.

Why the Company fought Mysore

Mysore controlled valuable trading routes and parts of the Malabar coast. The Company purchased important commodities, including pepper and cardamom, through this region.

Tipu Sultan sought to protect Mysore's commercial and political interests. In 1785, he restricted exports of selected goods through his kingdom's ports and prevented local merchants from trading with the Company.

Tipu also maintained relations with the French and sought military assistance for strengthening Mysore's armed forces.

The Company regarded Mysore as a major obstacle to its economic and political expansion in southern India.

The 4 Anglo-Mysore Wars

First Anglo-Mysore War, 1767–1769

The First Anglo-Mysore War involved Haidar Ali and the East India Company. It ended with the Treaty of Madras in 1769, which restored peace between the principal parties.

Second Anglo-Mysore War, 1780–1784

Haidar Ali again fought the Company. After his death in 1782, Tipu Sultan continued the struggle.

The war ended with the Treaty of Mangalore in 1784. Neither side had secured complete victory over the other.

Third Anglo-Mysore War, 1790–1792

During the Third Anglo-Mysore War, the Company fought Tipu Sultan with assistance from important Indian allies, including the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Marathas.

The war ended with the Treaty of Seringapatam in 1792. Tipu was forced to surrender substantial territory and accept other conditions, including the delivery of 2 of his sons as hostages to secure fulfilment of the agreement.

Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, 1799

The final war culminated in the Battle of Seringapatam in 1799.

Tipu Sultan was killed while defending his capital, Seringapatam, on 4 May 1799. The Company emerged victorious.

After the war, the former Wodeyar ruling dynasty was restored in part of Mysore under British protection. A subsidiary alliance was imposed, requiring the restored state to finance Company troops and accept Company control over major military and external affairs.

Why the defeat of Mysore mattered

The defeat of Tipu Sultan removed a major regional opponent of British expansion. The Company gained territory and strengthened its influence over southern India.

The result also reduced the opportunities for the French to use Mysore as an important ally against the English.

However, the fall of Tipu did not mean that the whole of Mysore was directly annexed. A reduced Mysore kingdom continued under the Wodeyars within the framework of British subsidiary control.

Prelims focus

  • Haidar Ali ruled Mysore from 1761 to 1782.
  • Tipu Sultan ruled Mysore from 1782 to 1799.
  • 1784: Treaty of Mangalore ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
  • 1792: Treaty of Seringapatam ended the Third Anglo-Mysore War.
  • 1799: Tipu Sultan died during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.
  • Trap: Tipu died in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, not in the Third War that ended in 1792.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 16–17, 2020–21 edition; IGNOU, Rise of Regional Powers, Unit 1, discussion of Mysore among independent regional kingdoms, consulted 20 November 2026.]
